analysis.one_liner: Cuts the top capital gains tax rate to 15% and lets investors qualify after holding assets just one month.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote, and not a single senator signed on.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cut the maximum tax rate on capital gains — profits from selling stocks, bonds, and other investments — to 15 percent, and would shorten the time an investor must hold an asset to get the lower rate from one year to one month. Capital gains tax cuts flow almost entirely to households that own significant investments, which skew heavily toward the top of the income scale. The bill was introduced by a single senator, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors with large taxable portfolios, who would pay a lower rate on their investment profits and could qualify for the reduced rate after only a month of holding an asset. Wealthy households capture most capital gains income, so they would receive most of the benefit. Frequent traders and the financial firms that process their trades would also benefit from a shorter holding period.

how_it_helps.text: It lowers the maximum capital gains rate to 15 percent, so investors would pay no more than 15 percent tax on their net capital gains.
It also applies the 15 percent rate for the alternative minimum tax on capital gains, preventing the AMT from clawing back the lower rate for investors subject to it.

It cuts the holding period for long-term capital gain treatment from one year to one month, letting investors get the reduced rate after holding an asset for just a month, which also applies to related provisions such as incentive stock options.
The changes would take effect for tax years ending after December 31, 2001.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers overall, who would make up the lost revenue. Because capital gains income is concentrated among the wealthiest households, the practical effect is a smaller share of the tax burden on high earners and a heavier relative burden on income earned through work. A shorter holding period would also encourage trading churn with little productive effect.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ordinary taxpayers via lost federal revenue

drawbacks.text: The bill was introduced without any cosponsors and received no committee hearing or vote, so it was never debated or scored on its merits.

Cutting the rate and dropping the holding period to one month would reward short-term trading; an honest supporter would have to acknowledge the revenue cost and that gains flow mainly to households at the top of the income distribution.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a small number of high-income investors, the benefit would be a substantially lower tax bill on investment profits. For everyone else, the cost is a narrower tax base and a larger relative share of the burden on wages. The one-month holding period tilts the code toward speculative trading rather than long-term investment, which even many capital-gains-cut supporters argue against. On balance the bill transfers tax burden away from the wealthiest households and onto the broader taxpaying public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 2001, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Zell Miller introduced the bill on August 2, 2001.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, and no further action was ever taken.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The broad taxpaying public is better off because the bill died: the tax burden on investment gains stayed where it was, and no revenue loss had to be offset. Wealthy investors are worse off only in the sense that they did not receive the additional tax cut.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary taxpayers; the proposed investor tax cut died

for.name: Sen. Zell Miller
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made no further recorded push for it; it received no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors from either party and no votes, so no partisan split on the bill is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Wealthy investors and capital gains earners
industries.note: The bill would have cut their tax rate on investment profits to 15 percent and shortened the qualifying holding period to one month; because it died, they pay the existing rates. Capital gains income is concentrated at the top of the income distribution, so the cut's benefits and the public's cost run in opposite directions.
A one-month holding period would have encouraged more frequent trading and more transaction volume for brokers and exchanges. The bill's death left the one-year holding period in place.
